content.text: In Claude Code, "think hard" and "be thorough" are ordinary prompt text. They can nudge Claude within its current effort level, but they can't lift it past that level. The controls are the effort level (
), the one keyword Claude Code recognizes (
). Pick them for the task, ideally at the start.

A webhook handler double-charges a few customers a week. You open Claude Code and write "Think really hard about this. Be thorough, take your time." Claude comes back quickly with a plausible fix: a lock around the charge call. It misses the actual cause, the payment provider retrying a delivery to a second instance. You add "ULTRA THOROUGH, CHECK EVERYTHING" and get a longer answer at the same depth. Meanwhile the session header has said "with medium effort" the whole time.
"To make Claude Code reason more deeply, tell it to think hard." Developers picked this up for good reasons:

items.text: It used to be standard advice. The docs say of their own list of retired tips: "Every one of these was good advice when it was written."
Asking a person to slow down and be careful works, so asking a model feels natural.
Wording really does change something. The docs confirm that phrases like these "can still nudge Claude within its effort setting".
Claude's answer often sounds more deliberate after you ask, which feels like proof.

content.text: The half-truth is the nudge. Wording moves Claude around inside a budget; it doesn't change the budget. As the best-practices guide puts it, it "won't lift it past it."

The platform docs add a detail that explains why higher effort feels different: effort "applies to every output token", so it shapes tool calls too, not just thinking. Lower effort also means "fewer and terser tool calls."
What your words do, and the one keyword
Claude Code recognizes exactly one keyword. Put
anywhere in a prompt and Claude Code adds an in-context instruction for deeper reasoning on that turn, without changing your session's effort. Typed in the terminal, it can also raise that turn to
(Claude Code v2.1.311 or later); when it does, the word shows in rainbow colors. Everything else, including "think", "think hard" and "think more", Claude Code passes through as ordinary text.
Words still matter for what Claude works on. A prompt that names the failure mode and the check to pass directs the effort; one that only asks for more effort doesn't.

The docs describe the trade in Anthropic's tests: at a higher level, Claude "tested more edge cases and verified more of its work before answering", and made more choices on its own. At a lower level it returned a starting point sooner, which suits work where you review each step.
is the deepest, but the docs warn it "may show diminishing returns and is prone to overthinking".

content.text: The second prompt uses the keyword for a one-off hard question and spends its words on the problem. If the whole session is hard debugging, raise the level instead, before you start:

content.text: Each model has its own prompt cache, so switching models mid-task makes the next request reread the whole conversation uncached. Changing effort does the same on most models; on Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5 and Fable 5.1 with an API key or a subscription, the cache survives. Set both before you start a task, and change them at task boundaries.
